rows.reference: Declaration of Modern Humanism (Amsterdam Declaration 2022), first principle, 'Humanists strive to be ethical'
rows.original: motivated by the benefits of helping and not harming
rows.says: Morality is part of the human condition, grounded in the ability of living beings to suffer and flourish, and driven by the benefits of helping and not harming. Humanists affirm the worth and dignity of the individual, and the right of every human to the greatest possible freedom and fullest possible development compatible with the rights of others. To these ends they support peace, democracy, the rule of law and universal legal human rights. They reject all forms of racism and prejudice and the injustices that come from them. Killing is not named, and no self-defence exception is stated.
rows.bearing: K1: taught by a wider rule (rule 7). 'Not harming', joined to the rights of 'every human' and the rejection of all prejudice, reaches everyone K1 protects, whatever their faith, status, sex or age, newborns included (rule 9), and it binds anyone, including heads of households. K1 is narrower than 'not harming' and allows defence, so whoever keeps the wider rule keeps K1. The sentence says what morality is driven by; it is not worded as a rule, so it is Clear teaching, not Explicit (as in Article I, row 13b). K0: taught by the same wider rule (rule 7). K3: 'not harming' every human, and support for peace and universal legal human rights in the same principle, reach people who are not fighting, but the text says nothing about conduct in war (borderline; see the K3 label).
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): three fresh searches in this pass restricted to humanists.international (searches 1, 2 and 10) returned the Humanists International page. The output shows 'morality is inherent to the human condition, grounded in the ability of living things to suffer and flourish, motivated by the benefits of helping and not harming'; 'the right of every human to the greatest possible freedom and fullest possible development compatible with the rights of others'; 'all forms of racism and prejudice and the injustices that arise from them'; the first principle titled 'Humanists strive to be ethical'; and the sentence supporting 'peace, democracy, the rule of law, and universal legal human rights', placed in the same first article. Not VERIFIED (direct): no local copy exists (source guide), and page fetches are not permitted.

rows.original: we feel a duty of care to all of humanity, including future generations
rows.translation: English original (Humanists International text; one member body's English copy reads 'towards all humanity')
rows.says: Personal liberty must be combined with a responsibility to society. A free person has duties to others, and humanists 'feel a duty of care' to all of humanity, including future generations, and beyond this to all sentient beings.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a supporting wider rule (rule 7). A duty of care to all of humanity includes not killing any member of it, and it reaches everyone K1 protects. It is a positive duty, and its verb is 'feel', a felt obligation that is softer than 'owe' (the previous wording of this row). Joined to 'a free person has duties to others', it is still a duty statement, so it supports row 1 rather than standing alone. The extension to all sentient beings is exclusion (e), context only.

rows.original: free of cruelty and its consequences, where differences are resolved cooperatively without resorting to violence
rows.says: Humanists are committed to treating each person as having inherent worth and dignity. They long for and strive toward a world of mutual care and concern, free of cruelty and its consequences, where differences are settled cooperatively without violence. They are concerned for the well being of all. All of this is put as commitment and aspiration, not as a rule.

It reaches each person and is stricter than K1 (no violence at all), so it does not clash with K1's exception; the tradition's bodies read non-violence as allowing defence (row 26). It does not name killing. K3: the hope for differences settled without violence is general, not about war (Implied for K3).

rows.says: Cites estimates that 5,000 to 20,000 women are murdered by family members each year in the name of honour, and urges states to make such violence a crime with proportionate penalties. The advocacy page lists honour killings among harmful traditional practices.

The joint statement is the only item found in which the Center for Inquiry itself condemns a private killing; it is outside the corpus and does not settle the branch question.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule)
K1.reason:
Deciding texts (all Tier 1, all VERIFIED (search), each re-searched in this pass on the issuing body's own domain):
- 2022 Declaration, first principle (row 1): morality is 'motivated by the benefits of helping and not harming'; it affirms the worth and dignity of the individual and the rights of 'every human', and rejects 'all forms of racism and prejudice'.
- The same principle's 'duty of care to all of humanity' (row 2, supporting; the verb is 'feel').
- 2002 Declaration, fundamental 1 (row 3, historic).
- For the AHA, Manifesto III (row 4, supporting): 'treating each person as having inherent worth and dignity', and a world 'free of cruelty and its consequences'.

Together these are Clear teaching of a wider duty not to harm. It reaches every person from birth, whatever their faith, status, sex or age, and binds anyone, heads of households included (rules 7 and 9). K1 is narrower and keeps a defence exception, so whoever keeps the wider duty keeps K1.

Why not Contradicted (rules 2 and 3). No counted text in any branch permits, commands or approves a private deliberate killing of any class of person. None declares such a killing blameless, and none grades protection by status. Manifesto II's abortion clause (row 28) is exclusion (c). Its euthanasia and suicide clause (row 29) is framed as an individual's own right, is weakly verified and has been superseded: exclusion (d).

Why not Unclear (rule 6). No counted text bears on K1 with a disputed meaning or a disputed judicial or private character.

Consistency with the cross-tradition hard cases. The nearest humanist analogue to Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 is the argument of Fletcher and Singer about disabled newborns (rows 18 and 19). These are individuals' writings, outside the corpus and unverified. No humanist body was found adopting them; search 12 found no humanist statement on the Groningen Protocol. Had a counted humanist text approved such a killing, the label would be Contradicted, as for a counted Stoic text. Nothing in any humanist text resembles a kinsman, zealot or master being declared free of guilt (Numbers 35:26 to 27, Psalm 106:30 to 31, Abu Dawud 4361).

Caveats.
1. The teaching is Clear teaching through a wider rule, not Explicit. No counted text names killing or self-defence. The Explicit statements (General Statement of Policy, row 13) are outside the corpus.
2. Every deciding row is VERIFIED (search) only. None can be read directly here, so under METHOD.md section 9, decision 6, the article cannot be admitted for this tradition until rows 1 to 4 are read directly.
3. Branches. The AHA is confirmed as a member of Humanists International, and its own Manifesto III teaches the same wider duty. The Council for Secular Humanism's own Tier 1 text (row 10) is search-verified only in part and shows no bearing in the parts seen. The Center for Inquiry's membership of Humanists International was not shown. If that branch is held to be separate and not bound by the Declarations, it is Silent on present evidence, not Contradicted or Unclear. This is the project lead's decision, and it should match Article I, where the Declarations spoke for the whole tradition.

K0.label: Taught (wider rule)
K0.reason:
K0 is narrower than K1. Killing for gain, or out of anger, hatred or revenge, is harm to a person, so the same wider duty in rows 1 to 4 includes it (rule 7). It reaches everyone, and it is now search-confirmed in this pass, including the rejection of all prejudice and Manifesto III's world 'free of cruelty'.

No counted text permits any such killing (rule 2 not met). None makes revenge for what the victim did a ground for blamelessness.

Outside the corpus, Humanists International condemns two kinds of private killing, and these explain but do not decide (rule 1):
- honour killings by kin, and laws that exempt the killers (row 15; jointly with the Center for Inquiry in 2013);
- the murder of atheist writers by zealots (row 16).

The same caveats as for K1 apply: the teaching is a wider rule at Clear teaching, not Explicit; verification is by search only, with no direct reading possible; and the Council for Secular Humanism branch question is open (Silent on present evidence if that branch is held separate).

K3.label: Taught (wider rule), borderline
K3.reason:
No counted text names non-combatants or speaks of conduct in war.

The support, all VERIFIED (search):
- 2022 Declaration (rows 1 and 2, re-confirmed in this pass): the duty not to harm and the rights of 'every human', the duty of care to all humanity, and support for 'peace' and 'universal legal human rights' in the same first principle. These reach civilians, children, the old and those who have surrendered (rule 7).
- Manifesto III (row 4): hopes for a world where differences are resolved 'without resorting to violence'. Now confirmed by exact-phrase search; it is an aspiration.
- Manifesto II (row 23, historic): renounces violence and force in international disputes and calls war obsolete. Now VERIFIED (search), no longer weak. This is a wider rule that includes K3, but it is in a superseded text and is addressed to the world community, so it supports and does not decide.

No humanist text in any tier approves killing non-combatants. The tradition's bodies accept defensive force (row 26, outside the corpus; row 27, Tier 2). Self-defence is aimed at attackers, so it leaves people who are not fighting protected.

It is borderline for three reasons:
1. The counted clauses are not written about war, so applying them there is the project's reading.
2. The explicit condemnations of targeting civilians (rows 13 and 24) are outside the corpus.
3. Every deciding row is search-verified only.

Rule 6 (Unclear) does not apply, because no counted text bears directly on conduct in war with a disputed meaning. If the project lead decides that a general non-harm clause does not reach conduct in war, the label becomes Silent. That decision must then apply equally to every tradition whose K3 result rests on a general non-harm rule (for example Jain and Buddhist non-harm).

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The K1 reason disposes of Manifesto II's clause on 'an individual's right to die with dignity, euthanasia, and the right to suicide' (row 29) partly because it 'is weakly verified and has been superseded'. Neither is a valid ground. Historic Tier 1 humanist texts are counted: corpus.md keeps Manifesto II in Tier 1 (flagged historical), and the households annex listed the historic 2002 and 1952 Declarations (HU-13, HU-14) among the texts deciding L2 as taught. A text cannot count when it helps and be set aside as superseded when it would hurt. Under METHOD section 9, decision 7, a later authority never outweighs a contradicting counted text, so supersession could not rescue the label if the clause did approve killing another person. 'Weakly verified' is also not a category under rule 1: the row is either verified, and counted, or unverified, and not counted. The only valid ground is exclusion (d). On the quoted wording the clause is framed as 'an individual's right', so it concerns the person's own death. The residual risk should be stated, not covered by supersession. 'Euthanasia' is not qualified as voluntary, and one of the Manifesto's own signers argued for ending some newborns' lives (row 18, outside the corpus).
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 (counted means Tier 1; there is no 'superseded' carve-out); rule 2; exclusion (d); METHOD section 9, decision 7; households annex L2 (historic Declarations counted as deciding).
objections.proposed: Delete 'is weakly verified and has been superseded'. Rest row 29 on exclusion (d) alone, because the quoted wording frames euthanasia as the individual's own right. Add a caveat: row 29 must be read directly. If its wording is not confined to the person's own choice, K1 becomes Unclear (rule 6), or Contradicted in one branch (rule 3), and supersession would not cure it. Flag for the project lead whether a body's declared supersession of its own earlier text counts as the tradition's reconciliation. It must be decided the same way for helpful and unhelpful historic texts.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The branch caveat is imprecisely stated and understates its consequence. (a) METHOD section 2 stops a text from showing what the whole tradition teaches only when a major branch rejects it. No row shows the Council for Secular Humanism or the Center for Inquiry rejecting the Declarations, so on present evidence, and as in Article I (row 13b) and the households annex, the Declarations speak for the whole tradition. The label is therefore consistent with precedent. (b) For the Council's own Tier 1 text (row 10), 'Silent on present evidence' overstates what was checked. Only the heading and opening of one section were seen, and the full text has never been read (it is also a recorded gap in Q-001 and the annex). Rule 3 distinguishes texts 'found silent' from texts 'not checked'; this one is in the second group. (c) The caveat does not say what follows if the project lead holds the Council to be a separate major branch that does not accept the Declarations. The tradition would then not clearly teach K1 as a whole, just as Digambara Jainism in Article I had to meet the floor through its own text (row 5c).
objections.rule_basis: METHOD section 2 (branch rule triggered by rejection); brief rule 1 (a text accepted by one major branch speaks for that branch); rule 3 ('found silent or ... not checked'); METHOD section 9, decision 3 (what a branch is); Article I note 5 (Digambara).
objections.proposed: Keep 'Taught (wider rule)' for the whole tradition, on the Article I precedent, with this caveat: 'For the Council for Secular Humanism, its own Tier 1 text has not been fully checked. If the project lead holds it to be a separate major branch that does not accept the Declarations, the result is Taught in the Humanists International and AHA branches and not shown for the Council, which does not meet unanimity until the 1980 Declaration is read in full.'

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The strongest case that K1 is too gentle runs as follows. The deciding clause in row 1 says what morality is 'motivated by'. It describes the grounds of morality and lays down no duty. Row 2's duty of care is only 'felt', and row 4 is aspiration. On that view no counted text teaches K1 above Implied, and the label would be Silent. The case fails, but the reason should answer it openly rather than leave it implicit. (a) Article I counted this same clause as Clear teaching (wider rule), row 13b, and decision D3 was settled on it for this tradition. Consistency requires the same rating here. (b) There is a second, independent route the reason does not use. A deliberate killing by definition denies 'the right of every human to the greatest possible freedom and fullest possible development', and no counted text accepts private killing. So the clause reaches killing by plain reference (decision 9), more plainly than it reached slavery in the annex. (c) On rule 9, the reach to newborns should be carried by row 1's 'every human' and row 2's 'all of humanity', not by 'person'. The humanist-adjacent argument for ending some newborns' lives (rows 18 and 19) works by separating 'human' from 'person'. Manifesto III's 'each person' (row 4) would therefore be the weaker text for newborns, though Fletcher and Singer cannot create a rule 6 dispute, because they are neither counted texts, classical commentators nor an authorised body.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7; METHOD section 3 'Wider rules'; section 9, decisions 2 and 9; rule 9; rule 6 (sources of a narrowing reading); Article I row 13b and decision D3.
objections.proposed: Keep the label. Add to the reason: the Article I precedent for the strength rating; the plain-reference route through the 'every human' right clause; and a sentence saying that rule 9 is met through 'every human' and 'all of humanity', which do not depend on the contested word 'person'.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The K1 reason says the 2022 Declaration 'affirms the worth and dignity of the individual'. Row 1's verification record lists the phrases confirmed by search: 'helping and not harming', 'every human', 'racism and prejudice', the heading and the support for peace and human rights. 'Worth and dignity' is not among them. The label does not depend on it, but the reason should cite only confirmed wording.
objections.rule_basis: Evidence standard: never rely on an unconfirmed reference or wording (brief Standards; METHOD section 3).
objections.proposed: Either drop 'worth and dignity of the individual' from the K1 reason for row 1, or mark it as not shown in the search output and to be checked on direct reading. The 2002 text (row 3) does carry the confirmed 'worth, dignity and autonomy of the individual'.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The consistency paragraph says a counted humanist text approving the killing of disabled newborns would be Contradicted 'as for a counted Stoic text'. De Ira is Tier 1 for Stoicism (corpus.md, section 8), but this row should not presume another tradition's final label, which another challenger may still change (for example under rule 4, if the passage is read as only presupposing the practice).
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2; rule 4; the need for uniform application across traditions.
objections.proposed: Reword it as: 'Had a counted humanist text approved such a killing, rule 2 would make the label Contradicted, the same rule that is applied to Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2.'

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The K0 reason only borrows the K1 reasoning. Manifesto III's hope for a world where differences are 'resolved cooperatively without resorting to violence' (row 4, confirmed by exact-phrase search) bears more directly on K0 than on K1, since killing out of anger, hatred or revenge is settling a quarrel by violence. This matters for the AHA branch if branches are ever split. The K1 caveats on row 29 and supersession do not carry over: neither the euthanasia clause nor the abortion clause bears on killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge.
objections.proposed: Keep 'Taught (wider rule)'. Name row 4's non-violence clause as the most direct counted support for K0 in the AHA branch. Say that rows 28 and 29 do not bear on K0. Keep the search-verification and Council for Secular Humanism caveats.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: Two statements about row 23 (Manifesto II, Thirteenth affirmation, Tier 1 historic) are inaccurate. First, 'No counted text ... speaks of conduct in war' and 'the counted clauses are not written about war' are wrong as worded: row 23 is written about war. What no counted text addresses is conduct within war (who may be targeted). Row 23 addresses only the resort to war, by the world community. Second, row 23 is discounted partly because it is superseded, which fails for the reasons given under K1 (historic Tier 1 texts are counted). The valid reason it cannot decide is different. It is a rule on how the world community should settle disputes, not a rule for people who are fighting, and it gives no guidance in the situation K3 addresses. Its rating, 'Clear teaching (wider rule)' for K3, is therefore too generous. The wider-rule test asks whether whoever keeps the wider rule keeps the narrower one, but an individual combatant cannot keep or break a collective renunciation of war.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 and METHOD section 3 'Wider rules' (the wider rule must bind the same agent); rule 1 (historic Tier 1 counted).
objections.proposed: Say 'No counted text speaks of conduct within war or names non-combatants; Manifesto II's Thirteenth affirmation (row 23) concerns only the resort to war.' Re-rate row 23 for K3 as Implied (resort to war, addressed to the world community; supports only). Give that, not supersession, as the reason it does not decide.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The K3 reason is inconsistent across rows. It treats row 1, a general clause on helping and not harming every human that is not written about war, as reaching non-combatants (borderline Taught). Yet row 4 rates Manifesto III, an equally general clause on 'treating each person as having inherent worth and dignity' and a world 'free of cruelty', as Implied for K3 on the ground that it is 'general, not about war'. That ground applies equally to row 1. Either both general clauses reach conduct in war, at the same borderline level, or neither does. This matters if the AHA is ever treated as a branch whose acceptance of the 2022 Declaration is not shown (membership was confirmed, a duty to accept the 2022 text was not). The AHA's K3 result would then rest on row 4 alone, and would be Silent or borderline Taught depending on this rating.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7; uniform rating of like texts (Article I independent-check finding that similar texts had been rated inconsistently); rule 1 (branch).
objections.proposed: Rate row 4 for K3 as row 1 is rated: Clear teaching (wider rule, supporting), borderline, not about war. State that, if the AHA were treated as a separate branch, its K3 result is borderline Taught on row 4.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The consistency sentence names 'Jain and Buddhist non-harm' as the cases that would fall with humanism if the project lead rules that a general non-harm clause does not reach conduct in war. This is the wrong comparison. The Jain and Buddhist first precepts are rules that name killing of living beings, so they reach killing in war more plainly. The humanist clause names neither killing nor war, and states what morality is motivated by, not a prohibition. The humanist K3 result is the weakest case of its kind, and the parity statement should identify the cases that are truly alike.
objections.proposed: Reword it as: 'That ruling must then apply equally to every tradition whose K3 result rests on a general clause that names neither killing nor war. Traditions whose counted rules themselves name killing (for example the Buddhist and Jain first precepts) are a stronger kind of case and would not automatically fall with it.'

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The strongest case that K3 should be Silent runs as follows. The tradition's own explanatory material says there is 'no single agreed humanist view of war' (row 27, Tier 2), and its bodies accept defensive war (rows 26 and 27). That suggests the counted non-harm clause is not read by the tradition as governing war at all. The case fails, and the reason should say why. The disagreement recorded in row 27 is about whether to go to war, not about targeting people who are not fighting. The defence the bodies accept is aimed at attackers, so it opens no exception for non-combatants. The IHEU's condemnation of 'the indiscriminate targeting of civilians' (row 24, outside the corpus) shows that the bodies read their principles as reaching civilians in war, though this explains and does not decide. The borderline status matches the households annex, where general freedom clauses were held to teach L2 'by principle, borderline' because slavery was not named.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 (outside-corpus and Tier 2 texts explain, do not decide); rule 6; households annex L2 precedent.
objections.proposed: Keep 'Taught (wider rule), borderline'. Add one sentence answering the 'no agreed view of war' objection, and cite the annex L2 precedent for the borderline label.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule)
K1.reason:
Deciding texts, all Tier 1 and VERIFIED (search):
- Row 1, the 2022 Declaration's first principle: morality is 'motivated by the benefits of helping and not harming'; it gives the right of 'every human' to the greatest possible freedom and fullest possible development, and rejects all forms of racism and prejudice.
- Row 2, the same principle's 'duty of care to all of humanity' (supporting).
- Row 3, the 2002 Declaration, fundamental 1: historic, showing the teaching is long-standing.
- Row 4, for the AHA, Manifesto III: 'treating each person as having inherent worth and dignity', and a world 'free of cruelty' where differences are settled 'without resorting to violence'.

Together these are Clear teaching of a wider duty not to harm. This is the same reading Article I accepted for row 13b under decision D3. A deliberate killing is harm, so the wider duty includes K1, and K1's defence exception makes K1 narrower still (rule 7).

There is a second, independent route. Killing a person by definition denies the right of every human to freedom and development, and no counted text accepts private killing. So the clause reaches it by plain reference (decision 9).

Rule 9 (from birth) is met through 'every human' and 'all of humanity'. These do not depend on the contested word 'person'.

Why not Contradicted. No counted text in any branch permits, commands or approves a private deliberate killing. None declares such a killing blameless, and none grades protection by status. Manifesto II's abortion clause is exclusion (c). Its clause on 'an individual's right to die with dignity, euthanasia, and the right to suicide' is exclusion (d), because it is framed as the individual's own right. That framing, not supersession or weak verification, is the ground.

Why not Unclear. No counted text bears on K1 with a disputed meaning. Fletcher and Singer (rows 18 and 19) are individual writings: outside the corpus, unverified, and neither classical commentary nor an authorised body. They cannot dispute or narrow a counted text (rules 1 and 6).

Caveats.
1. The teaching is Clear teaching through a wider rule, not Explicit. The Explicit statement (row 13) is outside the corpus.
2. Every deciding row is VERIFIED (search) only. Rows 1 to 4, and row 29, must be read directly before admission (decision 6). If row 29 proves not to be confined to the person's own choice, K1 becomes Unclear, or Contradicted in one branch. Supersession would not cure that while historic Tier 1 texts count (decision 7).
3. Branches. As in Article I, the Declarations speak for the whole tradition, because no row shows a branch rejecting them (METHOD section 2). The Council for Secular Humanism's own Tier 1 text (row 10) has been seen only in part, so for that branch the status is 'not fully checked'. If the project lead holds the Council to be a separate major branch that does not accept the Declarations, the result is Taught in two branches and not shown for the Council. That would not meet unanimity until the 1980 Declaration is read in full.

K0.label: Taught (wider rule)
K0.reason:
K0 is narrower than K1. A killing for gain, or out of anger, hatred or revenge, is harm to a person, so the wider duty in rows 1 to 4 includes it (rule 7). Manifesto III's hope that differences be 'resolved cooperatively without resorting to violence' (row 4) bears most directly here, since killing in anger or revenge settles a quarrel by violence.

No counted text permits such a killing. None makes what the victim did a ground for blamelessness (rules 2 and 5). The abortion and euthanasia clauses of Manifesto II do not bear on K0.

Outside the corpus, Humanists International condemns honour killings by kin and the laws that exempt the killers (row 15, jointly with the Center for Inquiry in 2013), and the murder of atheist writers by zealots (row 16). These explain but do not decide (rule 1).

Caveats as for K1: Clear teaching through a wider rule, not Explicit; search verification only; and the Council for Secular Humanism's own Tier 1 text is not fully checked, so the branch question is the project lead's, with the consequence stated under K1.

K3.label: Taught (wider rule), borderline
K3.reason:
No counted text speaks of conduct within war or names non-combatants.

The support:
- The 2022 Declaration (rows 1 and 2): the duty not to harm and the rights of 'every human', the duty of care to all humanity, and support for peace and universal legal human rights in the same principle. These reach civilians, children, the old and those who have surrendered, on every side (rule 7).
- Manifesto III's commitment to treat each person as having inherent worth and dignity, and to a world free of cruelty and violence (row 4). It reaches them in the same way and is rated alike: supporting, borderline.
- Manifesto II's Thirteenth affirmation (row 23, Tier 1 historic) is about war, but only the resort to war by the world community, not conduct in it. It is Implied for K3 and supports only.

The tradition's bodies accept defensive force (row 26, outside the corpus; row 27, Tier 2). Defence is aimed at attackers, so it opens no exception for people who are not fighting. The view in row 27 that humanists have no agreed view of war concerns whether to fight, not whom to target. The IHEU's condemnation of 'the indiscriminate targeting of civilians' (row 24, outside the corpus) shows the bodies read their principles as reaching civilians in war; it explains and does not decide.

No text in any tier approves killing non-combatants, so it is not Contradicted. No counted text bears on conduct in war with a disputed meaning, so it is not Unclear (rule 6).

It is borderline for three reasons:
1. The deciding clauses are not written about war, so applying them there is the project's reading. This is as for the freedom clauses and slavery in the households annex (L2, borderline).
2. The explicit condemnations (rows 13 and 24) are outside the corpus.
3. Every deciding row is search-verified only.

If the project lead rules that a general clause naming neither killing nor war does not reach conduct in war, the label becomes Silent. That ruling must apply to every tradition whose K3 result rests on such a clause. Traditions whose counted rules name killing itself are a stronger kind of case.
